subject: Pathology
summary: The Coombs test detects antibodies or complement bound to red blood cells, distinguishing immune from non‑immune hemolysis. It guides transfusion safety and evaluation of hemolytic disease of the newborn.

sections.p: The Coombs test uses anti‑human globulin to reveal immunoglobulin or complement attached to red cells. A positive direct test means in‑vivo coating; a positive indirect test shows serum antibodies that can bind transfused cells.
b: Direct Coombs = detects bound antibodies/complement on patient RBCs
Indirect Coombs = detects free antibodies in serum that could cause transfusion reactions

t.b: Is there antibody/complement already on the patient’s RBCs? Positive = immune hemolysis (e.g., AIHA, HDN). Negative = non‑immune causes.
Does the patient’s serum contain antibodies that could react with donor RBCs? Positive = risk of transfusion reaction or hemolytic disease of the newborn. Negative = low risk.

sections.p: Immune hemolysis occurs when antibodies target red cells. Common triggers differ by setting.
b: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm IgG, cold IgM)
Hemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh, ABO incompatibility)
Drug‑induced immune hemolysis (e.g., penicillin, quinine)
Infections: malaria, Mycoplasma, EBV (cold agglutinins)
Transfusion reactions (allo‑antibodies)
Parasitic diseases (schistosomiasis) and HIV can produce auto‑antibodies in low‑resource areas

sections.p: Patients may have jaundice, dark urine, anemia‑related fatigue, or splenomegaly. In newborns, severe anemia and bilirubin rise can cause kernicterus.
b: Pallor, tachycardia, dyspnea from anemia
Yellow sclerae, pruritic skin from bilirubin
Hemoglobinuria after transfusion

sections.p: Beyond Coombs, labs assess hemolysis severity and search for underlying triggers.
b: CBC with reticulocyte count – shows marrow response
LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin – quantify hemolysis
Peripheral smear – spherocytes, schistocytes

t.b: Is there free hemoglobin scavenging? Low = ongoing hemolysis.
Is cell breakdown elevated? High supports hemolysis.
What cell morphology is present? Spherocytes suggest immune hemolysis; schistocytes suggest mechanical destruction.

sections.p: Severe hemolysis can rapidly deplete hemoglobin and cause organ injury.
b: Hemoglobin <5 g/dL → cardiac failure
Rapid bilirubin rise in neonates → kernicterus
Acute renal failure from hemoglobinuria

sections.p: Treat the underlying immune cause, stop offending drugs, and support the patient while monitoring hemolysis.
b: Corticosteroids for warm AIHA – suppress antibody production
Rituximab for refractory cases – depletes B‑cells
IVIG for cold agglutinin disease or severe neonatal hemolysis – blocks Fc receptors
Transfusion of antigen‑negative, cross‑matched RBCs when life‑threatening anemia persists
Avoid cold exposure in cold‑agglutinin disease

sections.p: Regular monitoring of hemoglobin, bilirubin, and antibody titers prevents recurrence and guides transfusion planning.
b: Repeat DAT after treatment to confirm clearance
Educate patients about drug triggers and need for medical alert identification
In pregnant women, screen for Rh antibodies early and give anti‑D immunoglobulin prophylaxis

sections.p: Conditions that cause anemia but are not immune mediated.
b: G6PD deficiency – enzyme‑mediated hemolysis, DAT negative
Sickle cell crisis – mechanical sickling, DAT negative
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia – schistocytes, DAT negative

sections.p: False‑negative or false‑positive Coombs results occur under certain conditions.
b: Low‑temperature testing (4 °C) may detect cold IgM that disappears at 37 °C, leading to misinterpretation
Very low antibody levels can be missed – repeat testing if suspicion remains
Recent transfusion may mask patient antibodies

whenToSeekHelp: Newborn bilirubin >20 mg/dL or rising >5 mg/dL per hour
Acute renal failure with dark urine

faq.q: What is the difference between direct and indirect Coombs tests?
faq.a: Direct detects antibodies already bound to the patient’s red cells; indirect detects free antibodies in serum that could bind donor cells.

faq.q: Why can a Coombs test be positive at 4 °C but negative at 37 °C?
faq.a: Cold‑reactive IgM antibodies bind best at low temperature; they dissociate at body temperature, so the test may turn negative at 37 °C.
To Rh‑negative mothers after an Rh‑positive fetus or after any event that may cause fetal‑maternal blood mixing, preventing sensitisation.

exam: Explain how a positive direct Coombs test distinguishes autoimmune hemolytic anemia from G6PD deficiency.
List the first‑line treatment for warm AIHA and the rationale behind it.
Interpret a scenario where the indirect Coombs test is positive but the direct test is negative in a transfusion setting.
